title: Cora's Covers and the Wind
markdown:
The air in Oakhaven Canal Town always held a whisper of what might happen next, but on Book Festival day it practically hummed. Cobblestones, still damp from morning rain, gleamed under paper lanterns strung between stalls. For Cora, a young deer whose ears twitched at the faintest sound, it was a symphony of the delightful and the daunting. Today, for the first time, her work was on display in the grand tailoring competition.

A flutter began in her chest, a trapped moth doing quiet loops. Her greatest hope was to be utterly unembarrassed: no dropped stitches like little sad tears, no crooked seams sagging like a tired fence post, no material that wrinkled if anyone looked too hard. She had spent months on her entry — a collection of carefully tailored book covers, miniature art meant to guard cherished stories from damp canal air and the occasional barge splash. Sturdy linen, lined with soft wool, embroidered with scenes from classic tales.

She kept glancing at Elara. The name felt smooth, like polished wood. Elara was Oakhaven’s rising star tailor, known for precision and an effortless style that made even a simple apron look elegant. Cora watched her adjust a delicate silk ribbon on embroidered bookmarks that seemed to shimmer with an inner light. Elara moved with a quiet grace Cora’s twitching hooves could only dream of. She was not showy or proud. That was the problem. Elara was just good — so undeniably good Cora could not muster real annoyance. It was like being cross with a perfectly brewed cup of tea.

“Need a hand, Cora?” A gruff earthy voice startled her. Ned the mole, fur always dusted with something fine and shimmery, popped his head out from under a table piled with old atlases. His small dark eyes twinkled. “Saw you wrestling with that indigo velvet earlier. Nearly took a tumble into those rather dramatic poetry anthologies. That would have been a wrinkle you couldn’t have tailored out.”

Cora’s ears drooped. “Oh, Ned. I want everything to be perfect. Elara’s display is already so put together. Like a picture from a catalogue. Mine looks like it was assembled by a squirrel with a sewing needle.”

Ned snorted, a puff of dust that tickled her whiskers. “Elara’s always put together. Like a perfectly baked loaf. Good, solid, reliable, maybe a bit predictable. You, Cora, you’ve got the sparkle. You just have to let it shine, not hide it under a pile of worry. That worry is like a moth to your finest silk — it’ll eat holes right through your confidence.” He knotted a stray thread on her prize piece, a book cover depicting a dragon, with a single deft tug. “There. Good as new. Or good as it was. Which was very good. That dragon looks ready to breathe fire, not weep from a loose stitch.”

Cora managed a genuine small smile. Ned’s practical, slightly odd help was always a comfort. He had once produced a rare shade of silken thread dyed with forgotten berries from his “secret subterranean stash” hours before a deadline. He mostly worked as a stagehand, keeping book stalls from collapsing, but he had an amazing eye for materials. He’d once explained ancient weaving using only pebbles and fallen leaves.

As afternoon went on, the sun painted the sky in colours a painter would envy. Damp cobblestones began to dry, glimmering like scattered jewels. Canal water mirrored the deepening sky. The air cooled, carrying old paper and damp earth. Cora had arranged her covers so they stood proudly. A small flicker of pride pushed through the hard soil of her anxiety. Lanterns waited for evening. The wind waited too, though she did not yet know it.

Then a change arrived with a sudden boisterous gust. It swept down the canal, playful and mischievous, with the force of a startled flock. It whipped through stalls, sending flyers spinning like dizzy dancers, rustling tent flaps like a thousand excited whispers. Cora gasped, ears flattening. Her carefully arranged covers, especially the delicate linen scenes, wobbled. Her heart leapt. This was it: the ultimate embarrassment. Ruined.

She braced, hooves in cobblestones — but before she could whimper she saw Elara. Elara, whose silk bookmarks were just as vulnerable, did not rush to her own work. She darted with surprising speed, fluid and sure, and braced a teetering stack of Cora’s most delicate linen swatches, preventing them from tumbling into a muddy puddle near the canal’s edge. She did not even glance at her own display. Focus entirely on Cora’s fragile creations. Quiet grace.

The knot of worry in Cora’s chest unravelled like a tangled thread finally smoothed. She saw Elara not as a rival, not as a threat to quiet ambition, but as decent. Truly decent. It was not about winning, about the most perfect stitches; it was about preserving beauty, shared vulnerability, simple kindness in a shared challenge.

“We are not in trouble,” Cora whispered, more to the wind than anyone else. “We are merely visible. And visible things sometimes need a little help to stay upright.”

Elara offered a small genuine smile, a brief warm spark in the gusty wind. The wind, having had its fun, began to subside. The sky went a breathtaking indigo, vast and deep, mirroring the glass panes of the nearby conservatory, which held the last daylight in a soft internal glow.

Cora took a deep breath of cool damp air. She grabbed a nearby heavy leather-bound tome, an ancient history with a particularly sturdy cover, and placed it firmly against her most exposed display, anchoring it. Then she turned, ears perked, voice surprisingly steady. “Ned! Can you help me secure everything? Not just mine. Let’s make sure all our beautiful work stays safe.”

Ned emerged with a triumphant grin, sturdy rope, strong twine, a small effective toolkit. Together they worked, quick and efficient: securing displays, tying tarps that had begun to flap like unruly flags. Elara joined, hands equally steady. Soon the three were a quiet determined team, actions louder than competitive whispers. Side by side, shared purpose, silent harmony.

As the last lanterns flickered to life, casting a warm golden pool on the damp cobblestones, Cora looked around. Her book covers stood tall. Elara’s bookmarks were secure, shimmer undimmed. The wind had been chaos, yes, but it had revealed something the lanterns had been trying to say all afternoon. The sky, now a deep velvety indigo, held more than a competition’s end. Three figures, rope and twine, covers and bookmarks, still visible — and upright.
